translation: The Great Treatise on the Regular Government of the Five [Phases] (五常政大論) says: that which is rooted in the center is called the spirit mechanism (神機); these are the animals, whose root and foundation lie in the center. The root and foundation are the Spleen, Stomach, and Kidneys. (This explanation of the classic is forced; the meaning of the classic is not like this. The classic text has two meanings: one speaks of the frame and members of animals, which obey the center, hence "rooted in the center"; the branches and leaves of plants grow forth below, hence "rooted in the exterior." The other speaks of the spirit, intelligence, thought, and deliberation of humans arising in the center, hence "rooted in the center," while the nutritive and defensive qi and blood circulate in the exterior, hence "rooted in the exterior." If the center is destroyed, there is no awareness; if the exterior ceases, there is no movement. It is not a matter of the Spleen and Kidneys. What the later Original Patterns of Disease (原病式) discusses is extremely correct.) When food enters the stomach, the Spleen distributes and transforms its qi and flavor, nourishing the five viscera and the hundred bones. Thus sour enters the Liver and nourishes the sinews and membranes; bitter enters the Heart and nourishes the blood and vessels; sweet enters the Spleen and nourishes the flesh and muscles; pungent enters the Lungs and nourishes the skin and body hair; salty enters the Kidneys and nourishes the bone marrow.
translator_notes: 營衛 rendered as nutritive and defensive qi (standard English Chinese medicine terms).
